## 1. What you'll build, and why

This is the pivot of the whole project. Until now `swiftml` has been a *front end*: source → tokens →
tree → "is this tree well-typed?" Now we add the **middle** — **SIL**, our Swift Intermediate
Language — and **SILGen**, the pass that lowers the type-checked AST into it. SIL here is *raw* and
**memory-based**, not SSA: every variable is a stack slot, exactly as swiftc's SILGen emits it before
optimization (Phase 4 promotes those slots to SSA). From here the pipeline is the real swiftc one:

```
Parse → Sema → SILGen → SIL → (Phase-4 passes) → IRGen → LLVM → native
                  └── you build SILGen here; SIL is what everything downstream works on ──┘
```

The reason SIL has to exist is the thing concepts 06–07 kept pointing at: **the AST is a tree, but a
program's control flow is a graph.** A loop jumps backward; an `if` merges two paths. A tree can't
hold a back-edge. SIL represents the graph directly, as **basic blocks** joined by branches — and
*that* is the form on which every optimization and every backend operates.

- **You implement:** the **control-flow lowering** in `silgen.ml` — `if`/`while`/`for`/`break`/
  `continue` becoming basic blocks and branches. The front-end (05–07) is given and complete.
- **Outcome:** `swiftml2 --emit-sil` prints verified SIL whose shape mirrors `swiftc -emit-sil`.
- **Out of scope:** *running* it — IRGen (SIL → LLVM) is concept 09. 08 stops at emitting SIL.

## 2. Concepts in depth

### Basic blocks and terminators — the CFG

A **basic block** is a maximal run of straight-line instructions with **one entry and one exit**:
control enters at the top, falls straight through, and leaves via exactly one **terminator** at the
bottom. Our terminators are `br bbN` (unconditional jump), `cond_br %c, bbT, bbF` (branch on a Bool),
and `return`. A SIL **function** is just a list of these blocks; block `bb0` is the entry. The edges
between blocks (who branches to whom) form the **control-flow graph (CFG)** — the same graph you saw
for a `while` loop in concept 06, now made real.

SILGen's whole job is to walk the AST tree and *build that graph*:

![SILGen lowers the AST tree into a SIL control-flow graph: an `if`/`else` becomes a `cond_br` diamond — entry branches to a then-block and an else-block, which both branch to a merge.](figs/lowering.png)

### Raw, memory-based SIL — and why we *want* the loads and stores

Look at the SIL for `let x = 1; print(x)`:

```
%0 = integer_literal $Int, 1
%1 = alloc_stack $Int   // x
store %0 to %1
%3 = load %1 $Int
%4 = apply @print(%3)
```

Every variable becomes a **stack slot** (`alloc_stack`), and you only touch it through `load`/`store`.
This is **raw SIL** — exactly what swiftc's SILGen emits — and it is deliberately *not* SSA: the value
in `x` lives in memory, not in a single-assignment register. That looks wasteful, and it is — but it
makes **SILGen trivial**: lowering a variable is "store on write, load on read," with no need to track
which definition reaches which use. The cleanup is a *separate, well-understood* pass — **mem2reg** —
that promotes these slots to SSA values, deleting the loads and stores. That's **Phase 4, concept 16**,
and it's where you'll learn SSA properly, by watching this exact memory-heavy SIL turn into clean SSA.
Splitting "lower correctly" (here) from "lower *well*" (later) is swiftc's raw-SIL → canonical-SIL
design, and ours.

### SILGen is a *builder*

SILGen threads a small **builder**: a current block you append instructions to (`emit`), a way to
make new blocks (`new_block`) and switch the cursor to them (`switch_to`), and `terminate` to set the
current block's terminator (only if it doesn't have one — so a block that already ended in `return`
isn't overwritten). Lowering an expression returns the **value** holding its result (`%n`); lowering
a statement emits instructions and, for control flow, *splits the block*.

The two halves:

- **Expressions → values (mostly straight-line).** A literal emits a literal; a `Var` emits a `load`
  of its slot; a binary op lowers both sides then emits the op; a call lowers its arguments, emits a
  `function_ref`, then `apply`. The one exception is `&&`/`||`: they **short-circuit**, so the given
  `gen_expr` lowers them as a small `cond_br` diamond that evaluates the right operand only on the
  deciding edge (the result merges through a stack slot). That's the same diamond you're about to
  build for `if` — read it first as a warm-up. (Lowering `&&` as a plain bitwise op would be a real
  bug: `i < n && a[i]` would evaluate `a[i]` when `i == n` and trap, where swiftc runs clean.)
- **Statements → CFG.** This is your part. The pattern is always: evaluate, **create the blocks** you
  need, `terminate` the current block with the branch into them, lower each block's contents, and
  `switch_to` wherever control continues.

### Lowering control flow (your job)

- **`if c { A } else { B }`** — a **diamond** (see the figure). Evaluate `c`; make a *then*, an
  *else* (if present), and a *merge* block; `cond_br c` to then/else (or then/merge if no else); lower
  `A` in the then-block and `B` in the else-block, each ending `br merge`; continue in *merge*.
- **`while c { body }`** — a **header** block evaluates `c` and `cond_br`s to a *body* or an *exit*;
  the body ends with `br header` — the **back-edge** that makes it a loop; control continues in
  *exit*. The block before the loop must `br header` to get in.
- **`for v in lo ..< hi { body }`** desugars to a counted loop: a slot for `v` initialized to `lo`,
  then a while-shaped loop testing `v < hi`, with `v = v + 1` in a separate **latch** block. The
  increment lives in its own block because `continue` must branch *there* (not to the header), or it
  would skip `v = v + 1` and loop forever. (Evaluate `hi` *once*, before the loop.)
- **`break`/`continue`** branch out of, or round, the innermost enclosing loop. SILGen keeps a stack
  of `(continue-target, break-target)` — `b.loops` — pushed on entering a loop body and popped on
  leaving; both statements read its head. The break-target is always the loop's *exit*; the
  continue-target is the *header* for a `while` and the *latch* for a `for`, which is exactly the
  distinction the previous bullet is about.

One subtlety the given `gen_block` handles for you: once a statement sets a terminator (a `return`, a
`break`), the rest of that block is **unreachable**, so it stops lowering there — you never append
after a terminator, and dead trailing blocks just stay `unreachable` (a valid terminator the verifier
accepts).

### Why SIL at all (instead of AST → LLVM directly)?

Phase 1 *did* go straight AST → LLVM, and it worked. SIL earns its place because it's the right level
for the work to come: it's **Swift-aware** (it will carry ARC retain/release, value-witness calls,
exclusivity — concepts LLVM has no idea about), and it's **structured for analysis** (basic blocks +
the CFG) so that **every optimization and diagnostic in Phase 4** — mem2reg, constant folding, DCE,
CSE, inlining — is a graph transformation on SIL, not a hack on a tree or a fight with LLVM. swiftc
also runs *mandatory* SIL passes before it ever reaches LLVM, and two of them are diagnostics rather
than optimizations: definite initialization, and the "missing return" check you already met in
concept 07 — which is why the oracle in §4 has to ask swiftc for SIL, not just a type-check. Build
the right IR once, and everything downstream gets easier.

> Oracle: `swift/lib/SILGen/SILGenStmt.cpp` is the direct analogue of your `gen_stmt` — `visitIfStmt`,
> `visitWhileStmt`, etc., each create blocks and emit `cond_br`/`br`. `swift/docs/SIL.rst` documents
> the IR; our version drops the verbose `$*T` address types, `@convention`, and name mangling.

### The SIL you emit

This concept adds no Swift syntax — the grammar is concept 07's, unchanged. What it adds is an
**IR**, so this is the vocabulary to keep in front of you: every form `--emit-sil` can print, and
which of them your holes are responsible for. All of it is `<-- new` (SIL starts here); `<-- yours`
marks what the `TODO(08)` cases in `gen_stmt` must produce, everything else being emitted by the
given `gen_expr`, `lower_func` and `lower`.

A SIL **function** is a header and a list of blocks; a **block** is a label, straight-line
instructions, and exactly one terminator:

```
sil @name(%0 : $T, %1 : $T) -> $T {            <-- new  (given: lower_func)
bb0:                                           <-- new  block label, bb0 is the entry
  <instruction>                                         zero or more, in order
  <terminator>                                          exactly one, at the end
}
```

**Instructions** — each names its result `%n`, numbered per function:

| form | meaning |
|---|---|
| `%n = integer_literal $Int, 7` | an `Int` (also `$Bool`, printed `true`/`false`) `<-- new` |
| `%n = float_literal $Double, 1.5` | a `Double` `<-- new` |
| `%n = string_literal $String, "hi"` | a `String` `<-- new` |
| `%n = alloc_stack $T  // x` | a stack slot for `x`; the result is its **address** `<-- new` |
| `%n = load %a $T` | read the value at address `%a` `<-- new` |
| `store %v to %a` | write `%v` at address `%a` (no result) `<-- new` |
| `%n = binop "+" %a, %b $T` | arithmetic and comparison `<-- new` |
| `%n = unop "-" %a $T` | negation — the only unary operator in the subset `<-- new` |
| `%n = function_ref @f` | a reference to a SIL function `<-- new` |
| `%n = apply %f(%a, %b)` | call it `<-- new` |
| `%n = apply @print(%a)` | the one builtin `<-- new` |

**Terminators** — the edges of the CFG, and where your work shows up:

| form | meaning |
|---|---|
| `br bbN` | jump to `bbN` `<-- yours` (the branch into a loop, the back-edge, both arms of a diamond, `break`, `continue`) |
| `cond_br %c, bbT, bbF` | branch on a `$Bool` `<-- yours` (`if`, the loop header) |
| `return` / `return %v` | leave the function `<-- new` (given: `Return`) |
| `unreachable` | a block control never enters — a **valid** terminator, and what a block keeps when both arms of an `if` returned `<-- new` |

Real swiftc SIL is the same shape with a great deal more ceremony. Run
`swiftc -emit-sil add.swift` on the two-line `add` from §2 and you get

```
sil hidden @$s3addAAyS2i_SitF : $@convention(thin) (Int, Int) -> Int {
bb0(%0 : $Int, %1 : $Int):
  %4 = struct_extract %0, #Int._value
  %5 = struct_extract %1, #Int._value
  %6 = integer_literal $Builtin.Int1, -1
  %7 = builtin "sadd_with_overflow_Int64"(%4, %5, %6) : $(Builtin.Int64, Builtin.Int1)
  %8 = tuple_extract %7, 0
  %9 = tuple_extract %7, 1
  cond_fail %9, "arithmetic overflow"
  %11 = struct $Int (%8)
  return %11
}
```

— names are mangled, every call prints its full `$@convention(thin)` type, `Int` is a *struct* whose
payload has to be extracted, and `+` is not one instruction but a builtin plus the `cond_fail` that
implements Swift's overflow trap (§ "Parity gotchas" in `CLAUDE.md`; we wrap instead, which is why
our `binop "+"` is a single line). Ask for the *raw* SIL with `-emit-silgen` and a `var` turns into an
`alloc_box`, each access is bracketed by `begin_access`/`end_access` for exclusivity, and `load`
carries an ownership qualifier (`load [trivial]`). Underneath all of it the block structure reads
exactly like yours: `bb0`, straight-line instructions, one terminator.

### The diagnostics you emit

**None — and that is the point of this concept.** SILGen runs on a program sema has already
accepted, so a lowering hole has no user-facing error to report: if `gen_stmt` cannot cope, that is
a compiler bug, not a source bug. What `--emit-sil` prints is either SIL or a diagnostic that the
*front end* (05–07) produced, because the driver runs lex → parse → sema and bails on errors before
SILGen is called. So the wording table for this concept is concept 07's, unchanged, and the oracle
in §4 tests only that the same programs are accepted and refused.

Two messages are new all the same, and neither is a Swift diagnostic. The given **verifier** walks
the blocks after you build them and reports a lowering that does not hold together — a branch to a
block you never created, a function with no blocks — as `SIL verification error: …` on stderr, exit
1. swiftc has the same idea in `lib/SIL/Verifier/SILVerifier.cpp`, where it is an *assertion*: a
failing verification aborts the compiler with a stack trace, because it can only mean swiftc itself
is wrong. Ours prints and exits so a cram case can read it; treat a hit as a bug in your `gen_stmt`,
never as something a Swift program should be able to cause.

## 3. Build it, step by step

One skeleton, `silgen.ml`, and one function in it. The builder
(`emit`/`new_block`/`switch_to`/`terminate`), `gen_expr`, the simple statements
(`Let`/`Assign`/`Expr_stmt`/`Return`), and `lower_func`/`lower` are given; the five `TODO(08)` holes
are the control-flow cases of `gen_stmt`, described one by one above. Use `new_block` to make blocks,
`terminate` to set the current block's branch, `gen_block` to lower a list of statements into the
current block, and `switch_to` to move the cursor.

Fill them in this order — each one is the next one's scaffolding, and §4 says which file goes green:

1. **`if`** — the diamond. It is the smallest case and the only one that needs no `b.loops`.
2. **`while`** — the same three moves plus the back-edge, and the first push/pop of
   `(header.bid, exit.bid)` onto `b.loops`.
3. **`for`** — `while` again over a slot for the counter, with the increment in its own block.
   Push `(latch.bid, exit.bid)`, not the header: the latch is what `continue` must reach.
4. **`break`** and **`continue`** — one line each, reading the top of `b.loops`. They cannot be
   tested before a loop exists, because nothing else pushes that stack.

Reference: `solution/silgen.ml`.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase2-types-flow/08-sil-silgen
```

Six cram files, one per hole (`make lab C=… T=silgen-if` runs one), a unit suite grouped the same
way, and the oracle — in the order you fill the holes:

- `silgen-memory.t` — **green before you start**, and worth reading first: it is the given
  lowering, and so the vocabulary the holes have to produce. `let`/`var` as `alloc_stack` +
  `store` + `load`, a parameter stored into its own slot, a call as `function_ref` + `apply`, and
  the `&&` diamond `gen_expr` already builds.
- `silgen-if.t` — `--emit-sil` on an `if`/`else` (then, merge, else; both arms `br` to the merge;
  the next statement lands there), an `if` with no `else` (the false edge *is* the merge), an `if`
  whose arms both `return` (the merge keeps `unreachable`), an `else if` chain, and the verifier.
- `silgen-while.t` — the entry `br` into the header, the header's `cond_br`, the back-edge, the
  two edges that name the header, `while false` (still three blocks — folding is Phase 4), and a
  nest.
- `silgen-for.t` — the whole desugaring, the named slot for the counter, `hi` evaluated **once**
  in the entry block (`0 ..< k + 1` puts the addition there, not in the header), and the latch as
  a block of its own.
- `silgen-break.t` — which block `break` names: the loop's exit in a `while`, the exit and not
  the latch in a `for`, and in a nest the *inner* loop's exit. Needs a loop hole first.
- `silgen-continue.t` — the same for `continue`: the header in a `while`, and the **latch** in a
  `for`, which is the case that matters — branching to the header instead skips `i = i + 1` and
  the program loops forever. Needs a loop hole first.
- `test_silgen.ml` (alcotest `silgen`) — the same rules against the `Sil.modul` in memory, one
  group per hole, so a case can ask what the printed SIL does not say: which block a `br` names,
  how many edges reach the header, whether the latch is the block that stores the counter back.
- `oracle.t` — **the headline**: 34 programs from `oracle-corpus.txt` (20 accepted, 14 refused)
  go to swiftc and to your `--emit-sil`, and the verdicts must agree. swiftc runs as
  `-emit-sil -o /dev/null`, the same stage we stop at, because "missing return" is a SIL-level
  diagnostic and `-typecheck` would accept three of the reject cases (§2).

A hole you have not started shows as `TODO` with the list of what it will check; a hole in progress
shows `FAIL` with, under each failing case, what the test wants and what your code printed. To look
at one program on its own:

```bash
printf 'for i in 0 ..< 3 {\n  if i == 1 { continue }\n  print(i)\n}\n' > m.swift
_build/default/phase2-types-flow/08-sil-silgen/tests/lab.exe --emit-sil m.swift
swiftc -emit-sil m.swift                     # the same shape, buried in ceremony
```

## 5. Benchmark it

Nothing to time yet (we don't run). But note *where* you are: SIL is the IR the **Phase-4 optimizer**
transforms and benchmarks. The memory-heavy SIL you just emitted is the *input* to mem2reg — the first
thing Phase 4 makes faster.

## 6. Exercises

1. **The `guard cond else { … }` statement.** `guard` is an early-exit: if the condition is *false*
   run the else block, which must leave the scope (`return`/`break`/`continue`). Lower it as an
   inverted `if` whose false edge runs the else block and whose true edge simply continues — there is
   no merge, because the else block never falls through. (The value-diamond for `&&`/`||` is already
   shipped in `gen_expr` — study it first; swiftc is your oracle.)
2. **A textual SIL parser.** Write a reader for your `--emit-sil` syntax so SIL can round-trip
   (emit → parse → emit). This is what makes a `--sil-opt` workflow possible in Phase 4 (run a pass on
   a `.sil` file).
3. **Critical-edge splitting.** A "critical edge" is a CFG edge from a block with multiple successors
   to one with multiple predecessors. Detect them; some optimizations require splitting them (insert
   an empty block on the edge). A first taste of CFG surgery.

## 7. Recap & what's next

You introduced **SIL** and wrote **SILGen**: the AST tree became a control-flow graph of basic blocks,
with variables in `alloc_stack` slots (raw, memory-based SIL) and `if`/`while`/`for` as `cond_br`/`br`
between blocks. This is the representation the rest of the compiler is built on.

Next, **09-sil-to-llvm** writes **IRGen** (SIL → LLVM IR) and finally **runs** Phase-2 programs:
`if`/`while`/`for`/functions execute, and the output matches `swiftc` byte-for-byte again — which is
a much harder oracle than this concept's, and it caught a real bug in the `for` lowering you just
wrote. Then **Phase 4** turns this raw SIL into fast code — starting with **mem2reg**, where those
loads and stores become SSA and you learn SSA for real.

## 8. Appendix — full solution

Mirrors `solution/silgen.ml` (the control-flow lowering). The shape to notice: each case
**creates blocks**, **terminates** the current block with a branch, lowers the branch contents, and
**switches** to where control continues; loops push/pop `b.loops` and add the back-edge.

```ocaml
| Ast.If { cond; then_blk; else_blk; _ } ->
    let c = gen_expr b cond in
    let then_b = new_block b in
    let merge = new_block b in
    let else_b = match else_blk with Some _ -> new_block b | None -> merge in
    terminate b (Sil.Cond_br (c, then_b.Sil.bid, else_b.Sil.bid));
    switch_to b then_b; gen_block b then_blk; terminate b (Sil.Br merge.Sil.bid);
    (match else_blk with
     | Some e -> switch_to b else_b; gen_block b e; terminate b (Sil.Br merge.Sil.bid)
     | None -> ());
    switch_to b merge
| Ast.While { cond; body; _ } ->
    let header = new_block b and body_b = new_block b and exit_b = new_block b in
    terminate b (Sil.Br header.Sil.bid);                     (* enter the loop *)
    switch_to b header;
    let c = gen_expr b cond in
    terminate b (Sil.Cond_br (c, body_b.Sil.bid, exit_b.Sil.bid));
    switch_to b body_b;
    b.loops <- (header.Sil.bid, exit_b.Sil.bid) :: b.loops;  (* break/continue targets *)
    gen_block b body;
    terminate b (Sil.Br header.Sil.bid);                     (* the back-edge *)
    b.loops <- List.tl b.loops;
    switch_to b exit_b
| Ast.For { var; lo; hi; body; _ } ->
    let lov = gen_expr b lo in
    let hiv = gen_expr b hi in                               (* evaluate hi ONCE *)
    let addr = emit b (Sil.Alloc_stack var) Types.TInt in
    Hashtbl.replace b.vars var addr;
    ignore (emit b (Sil.Store (lov, addr)) Types.TVoid);
    (* header -> body -> latch (v = v + 1) -> header.  The increment lives in its OWN
       block (the latch), and `continue` targets the latch — not the header — so it can't
       skip the increment and loop forever. *)
    let header = new_block b and body_b = new_block b in
    let latch = new_block b and exit_b = new_block b in
    terminate b (Sil.Br header.Sil.bid);
    switch_to b header;
    let cur_v = emit b (Sil.Load addr) Types.TInt in
    let c = emit b (Sil.Binop (Ast.Lt, cur_v, hiv)) Types.TBool in
    terminate b (Sil.Cond_br (c, body_b.Sil.bid, exit_b.Sil.bid));
    switch_to b body_b;
    (* continue -> latch, break -> exit *)
    b.loops <- (latch.Sil.bid, exit_b.Sil.bid) :: b.loops;
    gen_block b body;
    terminate b (Sil.Br latch.Sil.bid);
    b.loops <- List.tl b.loops;
    switch_to b latch;
    let cv = emit b (Sil.Load addr) Types.TInt in            (* v = v + 1 *)
    let one = emit b (Sil.Int_lit 1) Types.TInt in
    let inc = emit b (Sil.Binop (Ast.Add, cv, one)) Types.TInt in
    ignore (emit b (Sil.Store (inc, addr)) Types.TVoid);
    terminate b (Sil.Br header.Sil.bid);
    switch_to b exit_b
| Ast.Break _ ->
    (match b.loops with (_, ex) :: _ -> terminate b (Sil.Br ex) | [] -> ())
| Ast.Continue _ ->
    (match b.loops with (cont, _) :: _ -> terminate b (Sil.Br cont) | [] -> ())
```

## 9. Exercise solutions

### 1 — the `guard` statement

`guard cond else { stmts }` is an *inverted* `if` with no fall-through on the false edge. Lower it:
evaluate `cond`; `cond_br` to a *continue* block (the rest of the enclosing block) and an *else*
block; lower `stmts` into the else block — they end in `return`/`break`/`continue`, so the else
block terminates itself and there is **no merge**. Contrast this with the value-diamond used for
`&&`/`||` (already in `gen_expr`), which *does* merge because both arms produce a value; `guard`'s
else arm produces nothing and leaves the scope. swiftc is the oracle for the control flow.

### 2 — a textual SIL reader

Lex the `--emit-sil` output (it's a tiny language: `sil @name(...)`, `bbN:`, `%n = <instr>`,
terminators) and rebuild the `Sil.modul`. Round-trip property: `parse (emit m)` ≡ `m` (up to
renumbering). This unlocks `--sil-opt`: read a `.sil`, run a pass, re-emit — the Phase-4 workflow for
testing one optimization in isolation.

### 3 — critical-edge splitting

Build successor/predecessor sets from the terminators. An edge `u → v` is critical when `u` has ≥2
successors and `v` has ≥2 predecessors. To split it, make a fresh block `w` with `br v`, and rewrite
`u`'s terminator to target `w` instead of `v`. Several Phase-4 passes (e.g. inserting code "on an
edge") need this; it's the simplest CFG-rewriting primitive.
